questions.title: Does § 1216(a)(3)’s "shall … conduct an investigation" create a judicially enforceable duty, or is it still committed to OSC’s enforcement discretion under Chaney?
questions.question_body: The statute says OSC "shall … conduct an investigation" of arbitrary or capricious FOIA withholdings. That sounds mandatory. Yet the opinion leans on Heckler v. Chaney and treats OSC’s choices as discretionary for causation/redressability, and the district court also said § 1216(c) committed the decision to OSC’s discretion. How do courts reconcile mandatory language in § 1216(a)(3) with traditional nonreviewability of enforcement discretion? Would a § 706(1) APA claim (to "compel agency action unlawfully withheld") or mandamus ever lie to force at least the initiation of an investigation, even if remedies (corrective/disciplinary action) remain discretionary?

questions.title: Why isn’t AFL’s lack of FOIA records an injury traceable to OSC for standing purposes?
questions.question_body: AFL says OSC’s refusal to investigate DOJ’s alleged policy caused AFL not to receive FOIA records. The court says the injury is traceable to DOJ, not OSC, and the causal chain through OSC action, MSPB sanctions, and DOJ compliance is too speculative. I’m struggling to see why this fails even under the "relaxed" procedural-injury framework. If § 1216 exists to deter arbitrary FOIA withholdings, why doesn’t the absence of an OSC investigation count as a cause of the ongoing withholding, at least for redressability? Where exactly do cases like Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine and Hecate Energy draw the line on third-party causation in this setting?

questions.title: Can a requester claim informational standing to receive § 1214 notices when OSC investigates under § 1216?
questions.question_body: The panel says § 1216 doesn’t entitle AFL to any information, and that § 1214’s notice provisions don’t automatically apply to § 1216 investigations. But § 1216(c) says OSC "may investigate and seek corrective action under section 1214 … in the same way as if a prohibited personnel practice were involved." Doesn’t "in the same way" import § 1214’s procedures, including complainant notices? How do Carson v. OSC (6th Cir.) and any D.C. Circuit precedent treat whether § 1214 procedural entitlements travel along when § 1216 is the predicate? If they’re discretionary, what text or precedent makes them discretionary rather than mandatory?

questions.title: How do § 552(a)(4)(F) referrals under FOIA interact with OSC’s independent § 1216 authority?
questions.question_body: The district court held that OSC misread its authority by insisting that § 552(a)(4)(F) predicates (a court order, fees, and a finding questioning arbitrariness) were necessary to investigate, because § 1216 independently authorizes investigations. The D.C. Circuit didn’t reach the merits due to standing. For future cases, what’s the correct statutory relationship: is § 552(a)(4)(F) an additional, mandatory trigger in some circumstances, while § 1216 provides a separate, discretionary or mandatory authority otherwise? Is there any case law or OSC practice guidance that reconciles these provisions?

questions.title: Why didn’t the "relaxed" procedural standing doctrine save AFL’s claim here?
questions.question_body: The opinion cites Center for Law & Education and Florida Audubon to say procedural injury relaxes imminence/redressability but not injury-in-fact or causation, and requires a threatened concrete interest. AFL claimed a procedural right to an investigation plus informational harms. The court said AFL lacked a statutory entitlement to information (for informational standing) and failed causation/redressability for the FOIA records theory. In practical terms, what would AFL have needed to allege to clear the injury and causation hurdles under the procedural-injury standard? For example, would a statutory text clearly guaranteeing requesters certain notices/information during § 1216 investigations have changed the analysis?

questions.title: How does Haaland v. Brackeen limit redressability based on a judgment’s persuasive effect on nonparties?
questions.question_body: The panel says redressability turns on how a judgment binds the parties, not whether its rationale might persuade nonparties like DOJ or MSPB. Are there recognized exceptions where likely persuasive effects on nonparties can count toward redressability, or is Haaland establishing a categorical rule? How does that square with earlier cases that credited likelihoods of third-party reactions to government policies in assessing redressability?

questions.title: What was the appropriate remedy once the district court found OSC’s legal error but also found discretion under § 1216(c)?
questions.question_body: The district court said OSC erred by treating § 552(a)(4)(F) as a prerequisite but also concluded the decision to investigate was discretionary, so it remanded for reconsideration instead of ordering an investigation. Is remand the standard APA remedy under § 706(2) when an agency relies on a legal error in exercising discretion? Could the court have ordered limited relief, like requiring OSC to consider the complaint under the correct statutory framework but leaving ultimate investigatory action to OSC? How does this interact with § 706(1) claims to compel action unlawfully withheld?

questions.title: Does parallel FOIA litigation and rolling production undermine standing to force OSC action?
questions.question_body: The opinion notes DOJ is producing records in AFL’s FOIA suit and the sufficiency of that production isn’t at issue here. Does the fact that AFL has an independent avenue for relief against DOJ (with actual production underway) defeat or diminish injury/redressability for claims seeking to compel OSC’s investigation? Would the standing analysis differ if DOJ had closed the FOIA request with no production, or if a court had already found an improper withholding but denied fees so § 552(a)(4)(F) wasn’t triggered?
